Crypto is not legal in India only to the extent that it is not a legal tender of exchange. Meaning, in India we cannot use crypto to buy or sell stuff and/or pay for services. However, investing in crypto is not illegal and the government can't ban people for investing in crypto.

So far, there was no clarity about taxation from crypto gains. Now there is. But the government has given a somewhat step motherly treatment to crypto investment and gains and the resulting taxation:

- Crypto gains/loss will always be treated as short term capital gains or loss, irrespective of the holding.
- The gains will be charged a flat tax rate of 30% + cess.
- Loss is entirely ours to bear
- Unlike other loss from sale of assets, crypto loss cannot be carried forward to subsequent years. This means that this year's loss can't be squared off from the gains of next year.
- Ditto for crypto gains.
- The crypto gains or loss cannot be clubbed with other income and/or STCG or LTCG or business income, etc. Pay the tax separately on such a gain.
- There are no tax slabs for crypto gains. Just a flat 30% tax (plus cess).

Now here is a further catch. The government has not said “crypto". The statement said Virtual Digital Assets. This is tricky and ambiguous. Obviously crypto is part of VDAs. But what else is included here? What about income from YouTube, Instagram, Tik-Tok and similar, QPP, etc. Do these also come under the purview of VDAs? Time will tell.

In India, you'll pay a 30% tax on profits from trading, selling, or spending cryptocurrency. Additionally, a 1% TDS is applicable on the sale of crypto assets exceeding ₹50,000 (₹10,000 in certain cases) within a single financial year.

According to the 115BBH section of the Finance Bill, a taxable event is defined as:

Conversion of any digital assets to INR or any other fiat currency.

Conversion of one virtual digital asset type to another may include crypto-to-crypto trading or trading in stable coins.

Paying for goods and services using a virtual digital asset.

As per the announcements on the taxation on crypto in India, the profits that will or have been incurred from the above transactions are subjected to a 30% tax, which is equivalent to India’s highest income tax bracket. Furthermore, if the transaction exceeds INR 10,000, the crypto tax will then have an additional 1% tax levied on them.

As per Section 206AB of the Income-Tax Act, 1961:

If any user has not filed their Income Tax Return in the last two years and the amount of TDS is INR 50,000 or more in each of these two previous years, then the tax (TDS) to be deducted for Crypto-related transactions will be at 5%.

30% tax on virtual digital assets (cryptos & NFTs) in budget 2022. What does it mean to India? Is it investor-friendly?\\
\\
Taxing a crypto transaction is to make it legitimate, however, it has taxation loopholes. If a crypto investor makes a transaction with his PAN card, then that transaction attracts a 1% tax deduction at the source. Further, the income generated out of that transaction attracts 30% tax. \* Is crypto & NFTs legal in India? - Not yet (we don’t have clarity) \* Are those transactions legitimate? - Yes by paying tax. As of now, we don’t have any regulatory mechanism to govern crypto transactions in India, we can only tax based on PAN card tracking. Broadly speaking, any transaction involving cryptos could be analyzed from two viewpoints – income and expenditure. Depending upon the nature and parties to the transaction, it’s 30% tax based on Income Tax Act, 1961 Assuming that the parties to the transaction are registered and situated within India and supplies are subject to tax, such transaction involving an exchange of cryptos for money or vice versa (for which separate commission is charged as consideration), would invoke 30% tax on the value of cryptos as well as on the commission charged However, this taxation process has loopholes \* Higher tax rate diminish their purchasing capacity \* The issue gets further complicated if the supplier or the receiver resides outside the territorial limits of India, i.e., in international transactions. (In US its 20% tax ,in India its 30% tax, in Japan its 40%) Moreover, this will be separate from taxes on capital gains from other sources like investment in stocks and funds, \* Similarly, crypto investors will also not be able to offset their losses from cryptos against any other source of income. \* Individuals (who aren’t investors) who receive cryptos as “gifts” will also be taxed 30%. So if your company pays “performance appraisal” in the form of bitcoin - you pay 30% of tax while your salary paid in INR still falls under normal tax slabs. The next issue is the valuation of crypto itself. The value of crypto is determined by translating the value at a point of time into the relevant unit of currency of the country (INR in India, USD in the US). However, crypto hardly fulfills a reliable ‘store of value’ function. The market value isn’t a true representation of accessible value to calculate tax. Say for example - if X buys bitcoins from Y on Feb 2022 and sells it on July 2022 - the tax will be valued as of Feb, not July as the invoice was produced dated Feb 2022. That’s tax value depreciation. This means the purchaser can produce the invoice whenever the value is lower, leading to low tax collection. This …. is a loophole during the taxation of cryptos. Binance-owned Indian exchange WazirX says crypto investment in India exceeded $43 billion in 2021, at a “1,735%” growth from 2020. Earlier such transactions fall under “business income” or “capital gains” For example, crypto transactions would be taxed as ‘capital gains’ if they are held with longer-term appreciation in value with fewer trades. Holding for less than 3 years would attract whichever rate is applicable under the prescribed brackets, and holding for more than 3 years would attract a 20% rate. Hereafter it’s 30%. So the govt thinks, investors will hereafter start “liquidating” their crypto portfolios and move to equity markets. However, the growth rate and returns are huge in cryptos compared to the share value growth rate. There are currently 810 currencies operating on at least 4,463 markets. Hence tracing transactions to the source is very difficult to produce and tax invoice. Thus, unless income is disclosed voluntarily or disclosure requirements are strictly enforced, it is hard to know if any income is being generated. Secondly, transactions take place across multiple jurisdictions, posing myriad difficulties in the enforcement of the rules and regulations \* Cryptos possess the traditional characteristics of ‘tax havens’, particularly because there is no specific jurisdiction in which they operate and are not subject to taxation at the source \* Furthermore, their operation is not dependent on the existence of a bank \* As a result, traditional methods of curbing evasion practices such as imposing regulations on financial intermediaries, due diligence, monitoring and reporting norms, etc. may be totally ineffective \* Transactions involving third party services located outside the jurisdiction (viz. bitcoin exchange services) may even escape the scrutiny of government entirely, encouraging money laundering and other malicious activities There’s potential for tax evasion due to lack of proper regulatory oversight - eliminating the risk of evasion practices and keeping a tab on taxing such transactions, would indeed be a challenge for the Indian government. So the real question is - is govt trying to move investors from cryptos to equity markets or promote tax evasion as higher tax rates increase the possibility of OTC markets (black market/grey market) With regard to NFTs - it’s still non-taxable worldwide. However, there’s not much clarity from the Indian govt as “ virtual digital asset” also includes NFTs apart from crypto - so does that mean NFT income attracts 30% tax ?? - No clarity from govt yet. Conventional taxation norms are ineffective to deal with cryptos. It’s practically tough to identify users, detect suspicious activities or even obtain records of transactions to tax them. Even international tax laws with bilateral trade agreements fail to formulate a proper tax structure for cryptos, as it involves multiple jurisdictions along with user anonymity. As of 02.02.2022 - the govt hasn’t passed the cryptocurrency bill yet (which may happen by April-May 2022), until then taxing crypto transactions would be a tough job for the govt. Regulated industries like banking or healthcare have a narrower design space than most AI teams realize. The constraints aren't just technical, they're legal. Here's what works in practice:

No data leaves the perimeter. This is non-negotiable for most regulated entities. If your agent compute runs in a third-party cloud, data flows through their infrastructure and that creates compliance exposure. The architecture needs to run entirely inside your own VPC: compute, logs, audit trails, and key management included.

Scoped, ephemeral credentials per workload. A single shared service account for all agents is a compliance and security liability. Each agent workload should get its own Open ID Connect (OIDC)-compliant identity at launch, scoped only to what it needs, revoked at teardown. This gives you both least-privilege access and a clean audit trail per session.

MCP Gateways instead of direct credential access. Rather than giving agents direct access to databases or APIs, proxy tool calls through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway authenticated by workload identity. The gateway holds the real credential, so the agent never sees it. This is especially important when agents call external services, keeping credentials out of the agent's context entirely.

Deterministic egress controls. Outbound traffic should be restricted to an explicit allowlist at the network layer. This contains the blast radius of a compromised agent and satisfies auditors who need to demonstrate that data can't be exfiltrated to arbitrary endpoints.

Full auditability. Compliance teams need to answer "what did this agent do, when, and under what identity?" Per-call logs tied to workload identity make that answerable.

After announcements by the Government during the Last Budget, as well as answers by MoS for Finance in the Lok Sabha, we now have more clarity on crypto taxation in India.

The tax rules announced so far include:

- 30% tax on income generated from transfer of virtual assets – effective from April 1, 2022.
- There will be no carry forward of losses into subsequent assessment years.
- 1% TDS on transactions – effective from July 1, 2022.
- If you gift cryptocurrencies or any other virtual digital asset, it will be taxed at the same rate at the hands of the recipient.
- The loss arising from the sale of any virtual assets cannot be set off against any other income from other virtual assets while computing tax.
- Infrastructure costs incurred in mining of VDA (eg. crypto assets) will not be treated as cost of acquisition.

While yet to formally legalize or define crypto, this definitely looks to be a positive step as India looks to regulate Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency in the country. We do understand and recognize that several people feel that the rules could have been crafted in a much better way, but we believe this is a good start and we should get more positive changes in the years ahead.

The Answer Nobody in Either Camp Wants to Hear

India's crypto adoption ranking and India's crypto tax regime are not in conflict. They're measuring completely different things — and understanding that gap explains everything.

* * *

What the adoption index actually measures

The Chainalysis Global Crypto Adoption Index ranks countries primarily on transaction volume, peer-to-peer activity, and retail participation — not on regulatory compliance or tax declarations.

India has 1.4 billion people. A young demographic. Cheap mobile internet. Deep mistrust of traditional investment returns. Aggressive marketing by exchanges. And a cultural appetite for high-risk, high-reward speculation that anyone who has watched an IPO listing day in Mumbai will immediately recognise.

People are buying crypto. Millions of them. The index captures that activity.

What it does not capture is how many of those transactions are being reported to the Income Tax Department.

That number is dramatically smaller.

* * *

The tax structure — and why it hits harder than the headline rate suggests

Section 115BBH introduced from April 1, 2022 imposes a flat 30% tax on transfer of Virtual Digital Assets — no slab benefit, no basic exemption offset, no deduction except cost of acquisition.

But the rate is almost secondary to the structural cruelty of no loss set-off.

If you made ₹1 lakh profit on Bitcoin and lost ₹80,000 on some altcoin in the same financial year, you pay tax on the full ₹1 lakh. The ₹80,000 loss disappears. You cannot set it off against the Bitcoin gain, against your salary, against capital gains from stocks, against anything. It simply ceases to exist for tax purposes.

This is not how any other asset class is treated in India. Equity losses set off against equity gains. Debt fund losses adjust against debt gains. Crypto stands alone in its punishing structure.

The 1% TDS under Section 194S on every transfer above ₹10,000 adds a liquidity drain that active traders feel acutely. For someone trading ₹10 lakh monthly volume, that's ₹1 lakh annually sitting locked as advance tax credit — capital that cannot be deployed.

* * *

So why does adoption keep climbing despite this?

Three reasons, and none of them are comfortable.

First, a large portion of retail crypto activity in India operates outside declared income. Peer-to-peer transactions, offshore exchange accounts, payments in stablecoins — none of this flows through Indian exchanges with KYC and 194S TDS. The adoption is real. The tax compliance is not keeping pace. In my practice, the number of clients who disclosed crypto holdings before 2022 versus after is telling — the law created awareness but also drove significant activity underground or offshore.

Second, small ticket investors below meaningful thresholds are genuinely numerous. Investing ₹500 to ₹5,000 monthly on CoinSwitch or WazirX, buying the narrative, not thinking about taxes yet. They're counted in the adoption index. They're largely not thinking about Section 115BBH.

Third, the speculative appetite simply overrides the tax calculation. If someone believes an asset will give 200% returns, a 30% tax on profits still leaves 140% gain. The math works until it doesn't — and when the market crashes, the no-loss-set-off rule delivers the final insult.

* * *

The compliance gap is where it gets serious

The Income Tax Department is not unaware of this gap. The AIS now captures data from Indian exchanges directly. Notices have been going out to people who showed crypto transaction data in their AIS but declared nothing in their ITR.

Foreign exchange holdings are a different and more serious problem. Accounts on Binance, Kraken, or Coinbase held by Indian residents require disclosure in Schedule FA of the ITR. Failure to disclose foreign assets — even crypto wallets — falls under the Black Money Act 2015, not the Income Tax Act. The penalty structure there is existential, not merely financial.

I have had clients come to me after receiving notices where the Department had traced USDT transfers through blockchain analytics. This technology is no longer theoretical — it is operational.

* * *

The policy contradiction is real and acknowledged

The government faces a genuine dilemma. A softer tax regime might bring more activity onshore, improve compliance, and generate more total revenue at lower rates. The current structure is pushing sophisticated money offshore while taxing unsophisticated retail investors who don't know better.

Several industry representations have been made. The budget has not moved on this for two consecutive years. The 30% rate and the no-set-off rule remain intact.

* * *

The honest takeaway

India ranks #1 in crypto adoption because of its population size, demographic profile, and speculative culture — not because its tax laws are friendly. The two facts coexist because a significant portion of that adoption is happening outside the tax net.

That gap is narrowing. Blockchain analytics, AIS data feeds from exchanges, and international information exchange agreements are making it narrower every year.

The people most at risk are not the large sophisticated traders who have already moved offshore. They're the mid-level salaried professionals who bought crypto during the 2021 bull run, made some profit, never declared it, and have since forgotten about it.

The Department hasn't.

If you're sitting on undisclosed crypto gains or foreign exchange holdings, the updated return window under Section 139(8A) still exists — and using it voluntarily is considerably less painful than responding to a notice.

Oh boy, where do I even start? After 8 years as an auto insurance agent, I have zero loyalty left to protect these companies.

These were our golden geese - we could raise their rates aggressively because they'd proven they wouldn't leave. The "File and Use" Scam Here's something most people don't know: in many states, insurance companies can raise your rates immediately and justify it later. We'd implement 15-20% increases across entire ZIP codes, knowing regulators would take months to review. By then, we'd collected millions in extra premiums.

Claim Frequency Was Irrelevant Your rates weren't really based on how often you'd claim - they were based on how likely you were to shop around. A customer with 3 claims who got quotes every year paid less than a claim-free customer who never compared rates. It was pure price discrimination.

We Loved Policy Confusion Complex policy language wasn't an accident. The more confusing your coverage, the less likely you'd comparison shop effectively. We'd change terminology between companies deliberately to make apple-to-apple comparisons nearly impossible.
